newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh airline says no problems with cargo plane.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh airline says no problems with cargo plane.

text.p: Kazakhstan's state airline said on Wednesday its Il-76TD cargo plane, which collided with a Saudi Arabian airliner in mid-air near New Delhi killing some 350 people, had been in good technical condition.
"We're only at the beginning of the investigation. We have very few details," Ildus Nazmutdinov, vice-president of Kazakhstan National Airways (KazAir), told Reuters in the Kazakh capital Almaty.
"The aircraft was in good technical condition," he said.
Nazmutdinov spoke just before he and other KazAir representatives left for New Delhi to meet Indian officials.
The KazAir plane was in collision with the Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747 on Tuesday in the world's worst mid-air disaster.

The disaster occurred two hours and 10 minutes after take off from Chimkent in southern Kazakhstan, KazAir spokesman Salir Mashanlo said. He said the pilot lost radio contact with air traffic control in New Delhi at 1300 GMT during the aircraft's descent.
Many of the 27 passengers on board, including one child, were Kyrgyz nationals. There were also 10 crew members.

Mashanlo ruled out speculation that the aircraft's instruments or the crew's English language abilities -- the international language of aviation -- could have led to the crash. "The pilot spoke English," he said.

Aircraft insurers Alexander Howden Aviation, a division of Alexander Howden Group Ltd based in Britain which insures some KazAir planes, said it was assessing if the Il-76TD, registration number 76435, was covered by the company.

"We are trying to clarify whether or not the plane was insured," Peter Tritton, a spokesman for the company told Reuters by telephone from London. "As it was a charter flight, it is not clear who assumes responsibility," he said.
KazAir said the plane had been chartered by Kosmokraft, a trading company based in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.

But while experts have yet to establish the cause of the crash, KazAir already has one of the worst reputations of the "babyflots", the myriad air companies spawned by the collapse of Aeroflot in 1991.

"Even if it wasn't their fault, this crash will have a bad impact on an already poor reputation," said one insurance expert. "KazAir have been trying to get cover but because of debts it's really difficult for them to do so," he said.

Dogged by financial problems, KazAir was formally closed down in August after being criticised by the government for falling safety standards and running up debts of $149 million. A new air company is in the process of registration.

One of KazAir's Tupolev Tu-154 passenger jets caught fire on take-off in Kiev in July, although no one was hurt. Many of the airline's flights suffered cancellations this year after the company was unable to pay for fuel.

Western investors flocking to the remote, oil-rich nation prefer to charter their own aircraft to fly over the vast former Soviet republic, about five times the size of France, rather than fly on the airline's ageing Soviet fleet.
